text: Several guides, both national and international, contain recommendations and guidelines for lighting implementations for all classifications of roadways. The most well-known and accepted specifications were produced by the Illumination Engineering Society of North America (IESNA), the CIE, and the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO), all of which base the merits of their guidelines on scientific research from an array of disciplines. These organizations have recommended minimum lighting levels, placements, luminaire types, and lighting trajectory guides to aid in implementation. While the addition of lighting is stated to have a net positive effect on safety, there are special considerations in terms of economy, glare, and distribution that are important and addressed in these guides. As an example, IESNA’s RP-8 suggests recommended lighting levels based on both measured illuminance and luminance. These recommended levels vary based on roadway classifications and pedestrian conflict as specific types of areas require different degrees of lighting uniformity and contrast (IES, 2014). 2.2.1.6.1 Color Contrast Nighttime driving presents many unique hazards that are not present during the day, specifically reduced visibility and contrast sensitivity. Contrast sensitivity is defined by how well an individual can visually separate an object from its background, an important aspect to night driving in terms of detecting objects or pedestrians in the roadway. There are two main types of contrast: luminance and color. Luminance contrast exists on an achromatic scale that is dependent entirely upon the amount of light reflecting from the surface of an object or its background and is the measurable difference between the two. Color contrast is the measurable difference between two colors. In general, night driving on an unlighted road removes color contrast from the equation due to the low light environment as human vision shifts from the photopic to the mesopic range. When roadway lighting is present, suddenly color becomes more important and color contrast increases visibility and safety. HPS light sources are currently the most prevalent street and roadway lighting sources even with the growing popularity of SSL. HPS systems are widespread due to their efficiency in output per watt of input power, their cost, and availability compared to other sources in the past. However, due to the sodium vapor in HPS lamps, the light it provides is colored yellow and the color- rendering capabilities of the lamps are not good. The color-rendering properties in the lamps can be improved by adjusting the pressure of the sodium vapor, but the lumens per watt efficiency is no longer economical. Studies comparing roadway lighting, specifically HPS and LED lamps of differing CCT determined that 5000 K luminaires, which consist of shorter wavelengths or bluer light, did not outperform the 4100 K in terms of color perception or detection distance. This led to the 11 determination that luminance does not directly correlate with detection distance and that contrast is the primary indicator of visibility (Clanton & Associates & VTTI, 2014).
